objectives: Define density and use ρ = m/V.

blocks.title: Density
blocks.md: **Density** is the mass per unit volume of a substance: $\rho = \frac{m}{V}$. Units: **kg/m³** or **g/cm³**. Water has density 1000 kg/m³ = 1 g/cm³. Hence **1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³**.

blocks.caption: ρ = density, m = mass, V = volume

blocks.title: Floating and sinking
blocks.md: An object **floats** in a liquid if its average density is **less** than the liquid's density, and sinks if it is greater. Ships made of steel float because the hollow hull makes the average density of the ship less than that of water.

blocks.title: Measuring density
blocks.md:
- **Regular solid**: measure the mass with a balance, the volume from its dimensions.
- **Irregular solid**: mass with a balance, volume by **displacement** in a measuring cylinder.
- **Liquid**: mass of a measured volume (mass of cylinder with liquid − mass of empty cylinder).

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- Always convert g/cm³ to kg/m³ (× 1000) or the reverse (÷ 1000).
- Volume in cm³ with mass in g gives g/cm³; volume in m³ with mass in kg gives kg/m³. Do not mix them.
- Density is not weight: a large stone and a small stone of the same material have the same density.

blocks.caption: Approximate densities of some materials (kg/m³).
blocks.alt: A bar chart: cork 240, ice about 920, water 1000, aluminium 2700 and iron about 7900 kilograms per cubic metre.

blocks.title: Example 1 — metal block
blocks.statement: A metal block has mass 540 g and volume 200 cm³. Find its density in g/cm³ and in kg/m³.
steps: Multiply by 1000: 2.7 × 1000 = 2700 kg/m³ (this is about the density of aluminium).

blocks.title: Example 2 — cooking oil
blocks.statement: Assume a cooking oil has density 920 kg/m³. Find the mass of 5 litres of it.

lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Physics — Density, pressure in solids, liquids and gases (to be checked against the official syllabus)

objectives: Define pressure and use P = F/A.
Use P = hρg for pressure in a liquid.
Describe atmospheric pressure and the barometer.
Explain the hydraulic press and calculate forces.
reviewNotes: Standard atmospheric pressure is about 100 000 Pa (101 kPa) or 760 mm of mercury; check which value the Board's questions assume.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Pressure
blocks.md: **Pressure** = force acting perpendicular to a surface ÷ area. Unit: **pascal (Pa)** = 1 N/m². A small area gives a large pressure: knives are sharp, tractors have wide tyres.

blocks.caption: F in N, A in m², P in Pa

blocks.title: Pressure in a liquid
blocks.md: Pressure in a liquid increases with **depth** and with **density**, and is the same in all directions at the same depth: $P = h\rho g$ (h = depth, ρ = density, g = 10 N/kg). It does not depend on the shape of the container. Total pressure = liquid pressure + atmospheric pressure (about $10^5$ Pa).

blocks.title: Atmosphere and hydraulics
blocks.md: The air has weight, so it exerts **atmospheric pressure**, measured with a **barometer** (about 760 mm of mercury at sea level). In a **hydraulic press** a liquid transmits pressure equally, so $\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}$: a small force on a small piston gives a large force on a large piston (garage lifts, brakes).

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- Convert areas to m² before dividing: 1 cm² = 0.0001 m².
- Liquid pressure uses the **depth**, not the total amount of water.
- In a hydraulic press the force is multiplied but the work is not: the small piston moves much further.

blocks.caption: A hydraulic press: pressure from the small piston (area A1) is passed through the liquid to the large piston (area A2).
blocks.alt: Two connected cylinders of different widths with pistons, a small downward force F1 on the narrow piston and a larger upward force F2 on the wide piston.

blocks.title: Example 1 — standing pupil
blocks.statement: A pupil of mass 60 kg stands on two shoes, each of area 150 cm². Find the pressure on the ground (g = 10 N/kg).

blocks.title: Example 2 — diver
blocks.statement: A diver in a lake is at a depth of 12 m (water density 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 N/kg, atmospheric pressure 10⁵ Pa). Find the pressure due to the water and the total pressure.
steps: Pressure due to water = hρg = 12 × 1000 × 10 = 120 000 Pa.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Describe how you would find the density of a small irregular stone using a balance and a measuring cylinder.
exercises.model: Measure the mass m of the stone on the balance. Half-fill the measuring cylinder with water and record the volume V1. Lower the stone in (tied with thread) and record V2. Volume of stone = V2 − V1. Density = m ÷ (V2 − V1).
exercises.rubric: 1 mark: mass by balance; 1 mark: volume by displacement V2 − V1; 1 mark: ρ = m/V.
exercises.explanation: Measure the mass m of the stone on the balance. Half-fill the measuring cylinder with water and record the volume V1. Lower the stone in (tied with thread) and record V2. Volume of stone = V2 − V1. Density = m ÷ (V2 − V1).

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: A density bottle has mass 30 g when empty, 80 g when full of water and 70 g when full of another liquid. (Density of water = 1 g/cm³.)

parts.prompt: Find the mass of water in the bottle.
Find the volume of the bottle in cm³.
parts.explanation: Water density is 1 g/cm³, so V = 50 ÷ 1 = 50 cm³.

parts.prompt: Find the density of the liquid in g/cm³.
parts.explanation: Mass of liquid 70 − 30 = 40 g in 50 cm³: 40 ÷ 50 = 0.8 g/cm³.

parts.prompt: Express the density of the liquid in kg/m³.
